steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on XRMDN, an extended recurrent mixture density network for short-term probabilistic rider demand forecasting in Mobility-on-Demand systems with high volatility. Explain why the problem matters, where existing forecasting methods and RMDN fall short, what we propose, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. MoD systems and why short-term demand forecasting matters
2. Characteristics of short-term MoD demand; existing forecasting approaches and their limits
3. RMDN and its limitations for MoD
4. Our proposed model and experiments
5. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. MoD + forecasting
- urban mobility: Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) systems reshaping how city dwellers navigate
- demand forecasting at heart of operational efficiency + customer satisfaction
- accurate predictions -> optimize fleet operations, better user experience
- car-sharing, ride-hailing: short-term forecasting critical, user requests unpredictable + highly volatile
- abrupt demand increases can overwhelm unprepared systems; disrupt supply-demand balance

2. Demand characteristics + existing approaches
- exogenous factors (spatial, meteorological) strongly influence demand
- significant unpredictable fluctuations; depends on temporal variables: weekday vs weekend, peak vs off-peak
- three frameworks: statistical, machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL)
- statistical: assume current demand linearly correlated with historical demand; linear regression; misses non-linearity of short-term demand, esp. high volatility
- ML/DL: learn non-linear patterns from historical data with internal + external cues
- but mostly point forecasts / expected demand; ignore uncertainty of future demand -> may hinder strategic planning + decision-making with dynamic demand

3. RMDN
- Recurrent Mixture Density Networks: probabilistic forecasting; approximates distribution of time series forecasts
- limitations for MoD: no exogenous info (spatio-temporal, meteorological); recurrent connections only in variance network, ignores demand auto-correlations in weight + mean networks -> may not use latent info in demand sequence

4. Our model
- new DL structure extending classic RMDN; short-term probabilistic demand with high volatility
- three correlated recurrent neural networks combined via demand residual -> trends + dependencies of rider demand
- end-to-end; approximates Gaussian mixture model with parameters from the three networks
- comprehensive experiments vs benchmarks: statistical, ML, DL
- first DL work on short-term probabilistic demand forecasting with high-volatility rider demand in MoD (to our knowledge)

5. Organization
- Sec. II literature review; Sec. III problem setting + Extended Recurrent Mixture Density Network (XRMDN); Sec. IV numeric study, two real-world datasets, three types of benchmarks; Sec. V summary + future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Urban mobility is changing, and Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) systems have become central to how city dwellers get around their environments, which puts demand forecasting at the heart of operational efficiency and customer satisfaction. Accurate predictions are needed to optimize fleet operations and to improve user experiences. Especially in MoD systems like car-sharing and ride-hailing services, being able to forecast short-term demand accurately is critical, because user requests are unpredictable and highly volatile. This volatility can cause big operational challenges, since sudden increases in demand can overwhelm systems that are not prepared, and this disrupts the balance between supply and demand.

Short-term demand for MoD systems has some distinct characteristics that time series models need to deal with to forecast accurately. First, exogenous factors like spatial and meteorological features have a big influence on demand levels. Second, the demand has significant and unpredictable fluctuations, mostly because it depends on temporal variables like whether it is a weekday or a weekend, and peak or off-peak periods. The existing methods for forecasting MoD demand fall into three main frameworks: statistical, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) models. Most statistical approaches assume that current demand is linearly correlated with historical demand sequences, and they use linear regression techniques for prediction. But this assumption does not capture the non-linearity of short-term demand, especially when volatility is high. ML and DL models, on the other hand, are good at learning non-linear patterns from historical data by using both internal and external information. However, these models mostly give point forecasts or expected demand results, which do not consider the uncertainty in future demand levels. This can make it harder to do effective strategic planning and decision-making when demand is dynamic.

- RMDN
  - probabilistic model approximating distribution of time series forecasts
  - limits for MoD: no exogenous info (spatio-temporal, meteorological); recurrence only in variance network, ignores auto-correlations in weight + mean networks
- Our model
  - extends RMDN; three correlated RNNs combined via demand residual
  - end-to-end; Gaussian mixture model with parameters from the three networks
  - experiments vs statistical, ML, DL benchmarks
  - first DL work on this problem to our knowledge
- Organization: Sec. II review, Sec. III problem + XRMDN, Sec. IV two real-world datasets, Sec. V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Urban mobility is changing, and Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) systems have become central to how city dwellers get around their environments, which puts demand forecasting at the heart of operational efficiency and customer satisfaction. Accurate predictions are needed to optimize fleet operations and to improve user experiences. Especially in MoD systems like car-sharing and ride-hailing services, being able to forecast short-term demand accurately is critical, because user requests are unpredictable and highly volatile. This volatility can cause big operational challenges, since sudden increases in demand can overwhelm systems that are not prepared, and this disrupts the balance between supply and demand.

Short-term demand for MoD systems has some distinct characteristics that time series models need to deal with to forecast accurately. First, exogenous factors like spatial and meteorological features have a big influence on demand levels. Second, the demand has significant and unpredictable fluctuations, mostly because it depends on temporal variables like whether it is a weekday or a weekend, and peak or off-peak periods. The existing methods for forecasting MoD demand fall into three main frameworks: statistical, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) models. Most statistical approaches assume that current demand is linearly correlated with historical demand sequences, and they use linear regression techniques for prediction. But this assumption does not capture the non-linearity of short-term demand, especially when volatility is high. ML and DL models, on the other hand, are good at learning non-linear patterns from historical data by using both internal and external information. However, these models mostly give point forecasts or expected demand results, which do not consider the uncertainty in future demand levels. This can make it harder to do effective strategic planning and decision-making when demand is dynamic.

The Recurrent Mixture Density Networks (RMDN) model is a probabilistic forecasting model that approximates the distribution of time series forecasts. But RMDN has limitations when it is applied to short-term demand forecasting in MoD systems. First, it does not encode exogenous information, like spatio-temporal and meteorological features. Second, in RMDN the recurrent connections are only used in the variance neural network, and the demand auto-correlations in the weight and mean neural networks are ignored. Because of this RMDN may not use the latent information in the MoD demand sequence.

To deal with these challenges, we propose a new deep learning structure that extends the classic RMDN to forecast short-term probabilistic demand with high volatility in MoD systems. In it, three correlated recurrent neural networks are combined through the demand residual to capture the trends and dependencies of rider demand. The proposed end-to-end solution changes the demand probabilistic forecasting paradigm by approximating a Gaussian mixture model, and the parameters of this model come from the three correlated recurrent neural networks. We also do comprehensive experiments that compare the performance of the proposed architecture with benchmark time series forecasting approaches, including statistical, machine learning, and deep learning models. As far as we know, this is the first deep learning-based work that studies short-term probabilistic demand forecasting while considering rider demand with high volatility in MoD systems.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section II we do a comprehensive literature review of time series forecasting approaches in MoD systems. In Section III we first briefly describe the problem setting of probabilistic demand forecasting in MoD systems, and then we present the proposed Extended Recurrent Mixture Density Network (XRMDN). In Section IV we do a numeric study with two real-world datasets to compare the XRMDN model to the three types of benchmark time series forecasting models. Finally, in Section V we summarize the work and discuss future research directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the changing landscape of urban mobility, Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) systems have become pivotal in reshaping how city dwellers navigate their environments, placing demand forecasting at the heart of operational efficiency and customer satisfaction. Accurate predictions are essential for optimizing fleet operations and improving user experiences. In MoD systems such as car-sharing and ride-hailing services in particular, the ability to accurately forecast short-term demand is critical because user requests are unpredictable and highly volatile. This volatility can cause significant operational challenges, as abrupt increases in demand can overwhelm unprepared systems and disrupt the balance between supply and demand [1].

Short-term demand for MoD systems exhibits distinct characteristics that time series models must capture to forecast accurately. First, exogenous factors, such as spatial and meteorological features, have a substantial influence on demand levels. Second, this demand is prone to significant and unpredictable fluctuations [2], largely because it depends on temporal variables such as the distinction between weekdays and weekends, as well as peak versus off-peak periods [3]. Existing methods for forecasting MoD demand fall into three principal frameworks: statistical, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) models. Most statistical approaches rest on the assumption that current demand is linearly correlated with historical sequences of demand, and apply linear regression techniques for prediction. This assumption, however, fails to capture the intrinsic non-linearity of short-term demand, particularly under high volatility. In contrast, ML and DL models are good at learning non-linear patterns from historical data by integrating both internal and external information. Even so, such models mostly yield point forecasts or expected demand results, which do not consider the uncertainty inherent in future demand levels. This may hinder effective strategic planning and decision-making in dynamic demand scenarios [4,5].

The Recurrent Mixture Density Networks (RMDN) model [6] is a probabilistic forecasting model that approximates the distribution of time series forecasts. However, RMDN has limitations when applied to short-term demand forecasting in MoD systems. First, it does not encode exogenous information, such as spatio-temporal and meteorological features. Second, in RMDN, the recurrent connections are applied only in the variance neural network, neglecting the demand auto-correlations in the weight and mean neural networks. As a result, RMDN may fail to use the latent information in the MoD demand sequence.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel deep learning structure that extends the classic RMDN to forecast short-term probabilistic demand with high volatility in MoD systems, in which three correlated recurrent neural networks are combined via the demand residual to capture the trends and dependencies of rider demand. The proposed end-to-end solution redefines the demand probabilistic forecasting paradigm by approximating a Gaussian mixture model whose parameters are obtained from three correlated recurrent neural networks. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive experiments comparing the proposed architecture with benchmark time series forecasting approaches, including statistical, machine learning, and deep learning models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first deep learning-based work to study short-term probabilistic demand forecasting while considering rider demand with high volatility in MoD systems.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we review the literature on time series forecasting approaches in MoD systems. In Section III, we first briefly describe the problem setting of probabilistic demand forecasting in MoD systems and then present the proposed Extended Recurrent Mixture Density Network (XRMDN). In Section IV, we conduct a numeric study using two real-world datasets to compare the XRMDN model with the three types of benchmark time series forecasting models. Finally, we summarize the work and discuss future research directions in Section V.

References:
[1] C. Yan, H. Zhu, N. Korolko, and D. Woodard, “Dynamic pricing and matching in ride-hailing platforms,” Naval Research Logistics (NRL) , vol. 67, no. 8, pp. 705–724, 2020.
[2] E. Chandakas, “On demand forecasting of demand-responsive paratransit services with prior reservations,” Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies , vol. 120, p. 102817, 2020.
[3] C. Ding, J. Duan, Y. Zhang, X. Wu, and G. Yu, “Using an arima-garch modeling approach to improve subway short-term ridership forecasting accounting for dynamic volatility,” IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems , vol. 19, no. 4, pp. 1054–1064, 2017.
[4] X. Chen, Z. Cheng, J. G. Jin, M. Trépanier, and L. Sun, “Probabilistic forecasting of bus travel time with a bayesian gaussian mixture model,” Transportation Science , 2023.
[5] I. Fatema, G. Lei, and X. Kong, “Probabilistic forecasting of electricity demand incorporating mobility data,” Applied Sciences , vol. 13, no. 11, p. 6520, 2023.
[6] C. Schittenkopf, G. Dorffner, and E. J. Dockner, “Forecasting time-dependent conditional densities: a semi non-parametric neural network approach,” Journal of Forecasting , vol. 19, no. 4, pp. 355–374, 2000.
